program_plain: World: a 128x128 lattice of cells (wrap-around edges, 4 neighbours each). Cells have 4 types (empty and species A, B, C; random start). Rules, in continuous time with random neighbour pairs: A replaces a neighbouring B with an empty cell, B does the same to C, C to A (rate 1 each); any species reproduces into a neighbouring empty cell (rate 1); any two neighbours swap places at rate 50.
model_family: Stochastic spatial cyclic dominance (May-Leonard rock-paper-scissors) lattice model with empty sites, reproduction and pair-exchange mobility (evolutionary game theory / ecology cellular automaton)
standard_name: Mobility-driven loss of biodiversity (single-species takeover above critical mobility threshold) in the spatial May-Leonard rock-paper-scissors model
citations: Reichenbach, Mobilia & Frey 2007, Nature 448:1046 - critical mobility threshold above which biodiversity is lost, below which spiral waves maintain coexistence
Frey 2010, Physica A 389:4265 (Evolutionary game theory: theoretical concepts and applications to microbial communities) - review of spatial May-Leonard model with sharp mobility threshold
Mobilia, Rucklidge & Szczesny 2016, Games 7:24 - influence of pair-exchange rate on spiral waves in spatial RPS games
Szolnoki et al. 2014, J. R. Soc. Interface 11(100) - Cyclic dominance in evolutionary games: a review (seen only as a reference-list entry)
Tainaka 1989 PRL 63:2688 and Frachebourg, Krapivsky & Ben-Naim 1996 PRL 77:2125 - earlier lattice cyclic predator-prey precursors (reference-list entries only)
searches: Mobility promotes and jeopardizes biodiversity in rock-paper-scissors games Reichenbach Mobilia Frey Nature 2007
cyclic Lotka-Volterra May-Leonard lattice mobility threshold extinction single species spiral waves review
notes: Critical mobility value (~4.5e-4) and the normalisation of swap rate to M were not verified in the search results; swap 50 vs 5 on 128x128 plausibly straddles the threshold. Finite-size and timescale effects matter below threshold. The 'activity rising' metric looks like an artefact of the metric's sign convention or a transient.
full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** The system is the stochastic spatial May–Leonard rock-paper-scissors model with a mobility (pair-exchange) rate. The behaviour you saw is the high-mobility loss of biodiversity, where one species takes over.

**1. Model family.** This is a stochastic cellular automaton, or individual-based lattice model, from evolutionary game theory and ecology. It is cyclic dominance in the May–Leonard form, which has four states (empty, A, B, C), and it is not the Lotka–Volterra form with conserved total density.
- Selection is the removal step, as in "A kills B, leaving an empty site".
- Reproduction into empty sites is a separate step. A separate reproduction process lifts the constraint of total population conservation.
- Mobility is nearest-neighbour pair exchange.

**2. The specific behaviour.** Your observation is that at high swap rate (50) a single type fills most of the lattice. The low-mobility variant (swap rate 5) is the other side of the same threshold.
- **Earliest clear source:** Reichenbach, Mobilia & Frey, "Mobility promotes and jeopardizes biodiversity in rock–paper–scissors games", *Nature* 448, 1046–1049 (2007).
  - The abstract says when mobility exceeds a certain value, biodiversity is jeopardized and lost, whereas below the threshold all subpopulations coexist and an entanglement of travelling spiral waves forms.
  - The mechanism is that when the typical length of rotating spirals becomes comparable to the system size due to strong diffusion, the system can evolve into an absorbing state where only a single species survives.
  - This is the same mechanism as the "one type fills the lattice" outcome. The spirals produce the cyclic changes in each cell's state. At high mobility they are lost, and the lattice then behaves like a well-mixed system.
- **Related reviews and follow-ups:**
  - Frey, "Evolutionary game theory: Theoretical concepts and applications to microbial communities", *Physica A* 389, 4265 (2010). The citation details come from other papers' reference lists. The text I retrieved is a LMU repository copy whose title is truncated. It demonstrates a sharp mobility threshold, with diversity maintained below it and jeopardized above it.
  - Mobilia, Rucklidge & Szczesny, "The Influence of Mobility Rate on Spiral Waves in Spatial Rock-Paper-Scissors Games", *Games* 7, 24 (2016). It treats the pair-exchange rate and spiral waves directly. I checked the title and venue against the search results.
  - Szolnoki et al., "Cyclic dominance in evolutionary games: a review", *J. R. Soc. Interface* 11 (2014). I confirmed it only from a citing paper's reference list.
  - Earlier lattice precursors: Tainaka 1989, *PRL* 63, 2688, and Frachebourg, Krapivsky & Ben-Naim 1996, *PRL* 77, 2125. Both are confirmed only as reference-list entries.

**3. Parameter check.** In the Nature paper the mobility is normalised by the number of lattice sites. I recall a critical value of about 4.5×10⁻⁴ from memory, and the search did not confirm it. Exchange rates of 50 and 5 on 128×128 = 16384 sites give M of roughly 3×10⁻³ and 3×10⁻⁴ under a simple normalisation. That puts 50 above the threshold and 5 at or below it. This fits your observation (extinction at high mobility, with the low-mobility variant expected to keep coexistence), but my normalisation is only approximate. Finite-size effects also matter: below the threshold, extinction times grow exponentially with system size, so a 128×128 lattice may still lose species over long runs.

**4. Metric oddity.** "g_activity_trend = -3.0 (activity rising)" is probably a transient or a bookkeeping artefact. As species go extinct and one domain coarsens, I would expect activity to fall, not rise. This is not a literature issue, but it is worth checking the metric's sign convention.

**5. Confidence: high.** The model, the swap-rate control parameter, and the single-survivor outcome above threshold all match the Reichenbach–Mobilia–Frey setup. The result is well replicated in reviews and follow-up papers.
